lines.name: Cash and cash equivalents
lines.why: Cash can repay debt or be paid out: a financial asset. Cash needed to run the business is operating; move it if you know how much.

lines.name: Receivables
lines.why: Owed by customers for sales: operating.

lines.name: Prepaid and other current assets
lines.why: Prepayments and other operating items: operating.

lines.name: Property, plant and equipment
lines.why: Assets used to produce and sell: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets
lines.why: Leased stores, offices and equipment used in the business: operating.

lines.name: Intangible assets
lines.why: Acquired technology, brands and customer relationships: operating.

lines.name: Deferred tax assets
lines.why: Taxes on operating income paid ahead: operating.

lines.name: Accounts payable
lines.why: Owed to suppliers for operations: operating.

lines.name: Accrued liabilities
lines.why: Services and other costs not yet paid: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease liabilities
lines.why: Rent owed on leases used in the business: operating by default. Move it to financing to treat leases like debt (if the balance sheet has no lease line of its own, they sit inside other liabilities).

lines.name: Deferred tax liabilities
lines.why: Taxes on operating income deferred: operating.

lines.name: Other current assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total current assets minus the current lines above: current assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other non-current assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Non-current assets (total assets − current assets) minus the non-current lines above: assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other current liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total current liabilities minus the current lines above: current liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other non-current liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Non-current liabilities (total liabilities − current liabilities) minus the non-current lines above: liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

s.t: We rely on data-driven performance marketing capabilities to drive return on our ad spend.

Successful execution of our strategy depends on our ability to attract and retain players, expand the market for our games, convert non-paying players into payers, attract and retain rewards partners, and offer unique and compelling experiences to players.
Our business relies on the sale, use, and redemption of virtual currency and digital items, as well as the processing of payments through third-party payment providers.
Our ability to operate our games and business depends on the continued availability, integrity, and security of our information technology systems and the data stored on those systems.

In addition, we rely on third-party service providers, including cloud infrastructure providers, analytics providers, marketing partners, and payment processors, to process personal information on our behalf.
Our business depends on developing, publishing, and continuing to service casual, “free-to-play” games that players will download and spend time and money playing.

Our monetization model depends on players’ willingness to make discretionary purchases of virtual currency and other in-game items, and is subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny, platform policies, and consumer protection standards applicable to in-game purchases and virtual currency mechanics.
Our ability to successfully develop games for mobile and web platforms and their ability to achieve commercial success will depend on our ability to:
A meaningful portion of the perceived value of our playAWARDS program depends on a limited number of significant rewards partners, including MGM.
We rely on a small portion of our total players for a substantial portion of our revenue and fluctuations in player engagement or spending could materially harm our revenue and operating results.

We rely on third-party hosting and cloud computing providers, including Amazon Web Services, and any failure, disruption, or significant interruption in these services could adversely impact our operations and harm our business.

In addition to hosting and compute services, we rely on third-party providers for data storage, content delivery, monitoring, and other infrastructure services, further increasing our dependence on external systems that we do not control.
Currently, we rely on third-party game development companies to provide operation and development services for our myVEGAS Bingo, POP! Slots, MGM Slots Live, and my KONAMI Slots games.

Much of the intellectual property we use in our games is created by us, but we also rely on licenses or rights we receive to third-party intellectual property for use in our games or platform to enhance the experience of our players or otherwise operate our business.
A substantial portion of our revenue depends on maintaining this perceived value among a relatively small number of highly engaged paying players.
Managing game economies is difficult, and relies on our assumptions and judgment.
Our ability to successfully attract in-game advertisers depends on the effectiveness of our advertising models and our ability to maintain player engagement.

We rely on third-party advertising networks, exchanges, and mediation platforms to source, serve, and optimize in-game advertisements, and changes to their terms, algorithms, pricing, or technical requirements could reduce fill rates, effective pricing, or advertiser demand.
We rely on a limited number of third-party infrastructure providers for hosting, data storage, and content delivery.

Our success depends on the security and integrity of the games we offer, and security breaches or other disruptions could compromise our information or the information of our players and expose us to liability, which would cause our business and reputation to suffer.

We rely on third-party service providers, including cloud hosting providers, analytics providers, and platform partners, and any security failure or disruption involving these third parties could adversely affect our systems and data.
We rely on a variety of third-party platforms and service providers to distribute, operate, monetize, and support games that incorporate sweepstakes-based promotional mechanics.

While our software and other proprietary technology may be protected under copyright law, we have historically chosen not to register copyrights for certain works and instead primarily rely on trade secret protection and contractual safeguards.

Our use of open source software is often subject to complex and evolving license terms, and our ability to comply with those terms depends on accurate identification, tracking, and management of open source components across our codebase.

To the extent that our games depend upon the successful operation of open source software, any undetected errors or defects in this open source software could prevent the deployment or impair the functionality of our games, delay new releases, result in a failure of our games, and injure our reputation.

In addition, heightened regulatory scrutiny of digital business models that rely on in-game purchases, targeted advertising, and virtual currency mechanics has increased the likelihood of investigations, enforcement actions, and civil claims in this area.

Recent legal developments in Europe have created complexity and uncertainty regarding transfers of personal data from the EEA and the UK to the U.S. We rely on approved transfer mechanisms, including the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework and standard contractual clauses, for certain cross-border data transfers.

Our business depends on our ability to collect, use, and share data to deliver relevant content, marketing, and analytics, and limitations on data collection or use could reduce our revenue and impair our business.

We also rely on third-party platforms, analytics providers, attribution vendors, advertising networks, and mediation partners to collect, process, and interpret certain player data, and any limitations, changes, or inaccuracies in these third-party tools or data flows could impair our decision-making and monetization effectiveness.

We rely on assumptions and estimates to calculate certain of our key operating and engagement metrics, and real or perceived inaccuracies in such metrics may harm our reputation and negatively affect our business.
Our rewards partners, content licensors, advertisers, and investors rely on our key metrics as a representation of our performance.
Analysts, investors, and regulators may also rely on these metrics in evaluating our business, growth prospects, and operating performance.

Substantially all of our games rely on data transferred over the Internet, including wireless Internet, and accordingly stable and timely Internet access is necessary to provide a satisfactory player experience to the players of our games.
Our business depends on the growth and maintenance of wireless communications infrastructure.
Our success depends on the continued growth and maintenance of wireless communications infrastructure in the United States and internationally.

Our ability to utilize our research credit carryforwards to offset future income taxes depends on our ability to generate sufficient taxable income before the expiration of such credits, and we cannot predict with certainty when, or whether, we will generate sufficient taxable income to fully utilize these carryforwards.
Even if we are actively covered by analysts, we do not control the assumptions, models or metrics that analysts or investors may rely upon to forecast our future results.
Our success depends on the performance and retention of our employees, including certain key employees.

In addition, our ability to execute our strategy depends on our continued ability to identify, hire, develop, motivate, and retain highly skilled employees, particularly in the competitive fields of game design, product management, engineering, and data science.
Our operations depend on cloud-based infrastructure and third-party service providers, and any disruption to their systems could adversely affect our ability to deliver our games and services.

The graph assumes an initial investment of $100 in our common stock at the market close on December 21, 2020, which was the initial trading day of the Class A ordinary shares of Acies (our predecessor) on a stand-alone basis.
